# Research Gap, Novelty Audit and Strengthened Contribution

**Assessment date:** 16 November 2026  
**Project:** Mobile-6G / provisional CLAPA framework  
**Status:** Evidence-based research design; no new empirical results have been generated by this project yet.

## 1. Executive assessment

The original broad claim — that privacy leakage accumulates across repeated RF/ISAC releases and should trigger adaptive release control — is **not sufficiently novel on its own**. Prior work already addresses sequential privacy, adaptive privacy-budget allocation for wireless sensing, finite-record Bayesian leakage in ISAC, CSI identity inference, and physical-layer privacy defenses.

The strongest defensible direction is an **empirical systems contribution**:

> A reproducible, release-history-aware privacy–utility–cost evaluation and control framework for sequential wireless sensing, using aligned identity and legitimate-task labels, explicit acquisition/session metadata, calibrated sequence-level attacker risk, and cross-environment/device evaluation.

The work should not claim a new universal leakage metric or formal privacy guarantee unless a separate mathematical result is derived and validated. The novelty must be demonstrated through the combination of (i) an explicit sequential adversary, (ii) calibrated operational risk measured over full release prefixes, (iii) an adaptive policy compared fairly with fixed and formal-DP baselines, and (iv) leakage-resistant evaluation across sessions and domains.

## 2. Direct-overlap audit: what is already known

| Research stream | Established contribution | Consequence for this paper |
|---|---|---|
| Sequential privacy and collusion | Adaptive privacy-utility optimization for sequential data requests and potentially colluding recipients has been studied. | Do not claim that adaptive sequential privacy is new in general. |
| Adaptive DP for wireless sensing | Adaptive privacy-budget allocation on CSI spectrogram blocks, clipping, calibrated Gaussian noise, RDP accounting and identity/membership inference evaluation have been proposed. | An adaptive threshold or adaptive noise budget alone is not a sufficient novelty claim. Include this as a direct comparator and distinguish user-level versus sample-level protection. |
| Operational leakage in ISAC | A finite-record Bayesian operational leakage metric separates prior side information from observation-driven adversarial success. | Do not claim first use of Bayesian success probability or finite-observation leakage. The proposed work should study sequential prefixes and empirical sensor-data attackers, not rebrand this metric. |
| CSI identity inference | Activity-agnostic open-set CSI user verification has been studied using Siamese embeddings and multiple holdout protocols. | Identity leakage from CSI is established. The gap is how that leakage evolves under repeated releases and how a controller manages it while retaining another task. |
| Age-aware sensing | Recent CSI sensing work encodes age/staleness under sparse sensing budgets and reports that temporal coverage matters. | Model release timing, packet gaps and staleness; do not assume uniformly spaced observations. |
| Physical-layer ISAC privacy | Constellation shaping, signal indistinguishability, beamforming/perturbation, artificial multipath and RIS-based defenses are active directions. | Position CLAPA as a release/feature-layer controller, not a new waveform or RF physical-layer defense. |

## 3. Strongest research gap

### Gap A — Sequential attacker risk is not the same as a per-window score

AUC from an isolated release does not quantify the attacker's success after jointly processing an ordered prefix of releases. Nor can AUC values be added to create a cumulative privacy budget. The study should report a risk trajectory across prefix lengths (K), using the same held-out acquisition groups and a sequence-aware adversary.

### Gap B — Privacy and legitimate sensing need to be evaluated on aligned records

A privacy claim is weak if the attacker and legitimate model are evaluated on unrelated records or incompatible splits. CSI-Bench appears promising because its multitask release contains identity, activity and proximity labels, and its directory structure records user, activity, environment, device and session. The first technical task is to confirm that the UID, HAR and proximity metadata refer to the same sample IDs/files before joining them.

### Gap C — Domain shift can change the privacy threat materially

A model may identify users extremely well in an in-distribution split yet perform very differently across devices or environments. The controller must be tested on session-, device- and environment-shifted data. A policy calibrated on one domain should not be assumed to protect another.

### Gap D — Adaptive control must be compared with formal privacy accounting

Adaptive DP feature release already exists. A new non-DP policy must be explicit that it provides empirical risk management, not a formal guarantee. The comparison should include a properly calibrated DP baseline where adjacency, clipping sensitivity, noise calibration and composition accounting can be implemented correctly. Report sample-level and user-level protection separately.

### Gap E — Operational feasibility and uncertainty are under-reported in many prototypes

A deployable policy needs latency, memory, release timing, packet-loss/staleness and calibration analysis. Report confidence intervals at participant/session level, not only per-window bootstrap intervals.

## 4. Recommended title and contribution framing

### Preferred title

**History-Aware Privacy–Utility Control for Sequential Wireless Sensing: Identity Leakage, Task Preservation and Domain Shift**

Optional subtitle for a 6G/ISAC venue: *A dataset-grounded evaluation framework for next-generation integrated sensing and communication.*

This title avoids implying that Wi-Fi CSI measurements are native 6G data or that the method already provides a formal privacy guarantee.

### Proposed contributions — only claim after experiments

1. **A leakage-resistant evaluation protocol** for ordered sensing-release prefixes, retaining participant, activity, environment, device and session metadata.
2. **A calibrated sequence-level adversary benchmark** that compares single-release, last-release, temporal-summary and sequence-model attackers.
3. **A history-aware release controller** that selects ALLOW / SANITIZE / BLOCK from validation-calibrated estimates of attacker success, legitimate-task utility and processing cost.
4. **A multi-domain empirical assessment** across held-out sessions, devices and environments, with participant/session-level uncertainty estimates.
5. **A reproducible comparison** against fixed perturbation, current-release-only control and a formally accounted DP feature-release baseline.

These are candidate contributions, not yet experimentally demonstrated findings.

## 5. Strongest dataset strategy

### Primary: CSI-Bench (NeurIPS 2025)

The NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks paper describes more than 461 hours of CSI recordings, 35 users, 26 environments and 16 device types, including a multitask dataset with joint identity, activity and proximity annotations. Its public data layout documents user/activity/environment/device/session directories and task metadata/split files.

- NeurIPS paper: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/f7c68372b3d39e8d7a093eb2edaaad87-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.html
- Project page and dataset link: https://ai-iot-sensing.github.io/projects/project.html
- Code and data schema: https://github.com/guozhen-jenn-zhu/CSI-Bench-Real-WiFi-Sensing-Benchmark
- Kaggle data entry: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/guozhenjennzhu/csi-bench

The project page reports a single-task user-identification accuracy/F1 of 99.51%/99.51% and multitask values of 99.83%/100.00% on its reported in-distribution evaluation. These are **the dataset authors' benchmark results**, not results produced by this Mobile-6G project. They motivate a privacy audit but must not be presented as CLAPA performance.

The repository's reproduced results also report substantial changes under cross-device and cross-environment tests. In particular, the reported multitask identity results include cross-device accuracy 0.2151 and cross-environment accuracy 0.1421; the cross-user split holds out unseen identity classes and is not a valid closed-set classification test. Treat these as author-reported baseline results and verify the current dataset release, split definitions and result provenance before quoting them in a paper.

**Dataset admission conditions:** confirm the Kaggle data licence/terms independently of the MIT licence on the code repository; inspect the latest dataset version; validate common sample IDs or file paths across UID/HAR/proximity metadata; check session multiplicity per user; check timestamp semantics and file integrity; preserve the official splits for baseline reproduction while creating additional leakage-resistant splits only with documented rationale. Do not assume the code licence also licences the dataset.

### Secondary: mmHSense (IEEE Access 2026)

Use mmW-GaitID for a separate mmWave person-identification replication and mmW-Loc for a distinct location-inference task, after inspecting the archive. The paper reports 20 participants and multiple collection days, but the paper's collection duration does not by itself prove repeated sessions per participant. Do not infer session IDs from days without participant-level metadata.

- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3691174
- Official code: https://github.com/nisarnabeel/Multi-Modal-and-Distributed-mmWave-ISAC-Datasets-for-Human-Sensing
- DataPort: https://ieee-dataport.org/documents/mmhsense-multi-modal-and-distributed-mmwave-isac-datasets-human-sensing

### Secondary validation: OPERAnet

OPERAnet contains approximately eight hours of RF/vision measurements from six participants in two rooms and is useful for an activity/localization sensitivity analysis. Its small participant count makes it unsuitable as the primary identity-generalization benchmark.

- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01573-2

## 6. Experimental design required to support the paper

### Threat model

- Protected attributes: participant identity and, in a separate experiment, location/proximity if labels support it.
- Legitimate task: activity recognition (or proximity when activity is not aligned).
- Adversary: observes released RF/CSI feature sequences, timestamps and explicitly stated metadata; no unreported access to raw sensor data.
- Knowledge: evaluate both known-sanitizer and unknown-sanitizer settings if feasible.
- Release horizon: (K in {1,2,5,10,20}), limited by actual recording length and release cadence.
- Identity protocol: known-enrolled identity re-identification across held-out sessions; separately, open-set verification for unseen users. Do not mix the two.

### Attackers

1. Single/last release.
2. First release.
3. Temporal mean.
4. Concatenated ordered sequence.
5. Mean/variance/trend/quantile summaries.
6. GRU or 1D-CNN only if sample volume supports it.
7. Side-information variants: activity-known, activity-unknown, device-known and environment-known, with the information disclosed for each experiment.

### Defenses and controls

- No sanitizer.
- Fixed Gaussian perturbation (not DP unless calibrated).
- Quantization and clipping.
- Fixed per-release threshold gate.
- Current-release-only adaptive gate.
- Proposed history-aware policy.
- Formal DP feature-release baseline with correct adjacency, sensitivity and composition accounting, if implementation is feasible.

### Primary metrics

- Utility: activity macro-F1, balanced accuracy and per-class recall.
- Identity: macro-F1, ROC-AUC, calibrated top-1 posterior success, and verification EER/TAR@FAR when using pairwise verification.
- Risk trajectory: report the empirical attacker success/posterior risk for each complete prefix (K); do not sum AUC.
- Calibration: Brier score, log-loss and expected calibration error; use validation-only calibration.
- Cost: per-release and end-to-end latency, CPU time, peak memory and model size.
- Uncertainty: at least five seeds where training is stochastic; paired participant/session bootstrap confidence intervals; effect sizes and correction for multiple confirmatory tests.

### Controller design

The controller should receive a calibrated estimate of adversarial success for the **entire candidate prefix**, utility estimate for the legitimate task and estimated processing cost. It chooses among ALLOW / SANITIZE / BLOCK subject to a declared utility floor and latency budget. Sanitizer strength and thresholds must be selected using training/validation data only. Recompute risk after sanitization before authorizing the release. The policy is an empirical risk controller unless a formal theorem and assumptions are supplied; do not call it a privacy guarantee.

## 7. Go/no-go gates

| Gate | Required evidence | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| G1 — Dataset rights | Dataset licence/terms and permitted research use verified | No raw-data use until verified |
| G2 — Label alignment | UID, HAR and proximity samples joined on stable IDs/file paths with no ambiguous duplicates | Otherwise separate task experiments |
| G3 — Temporal structure | Multiple genuine sessions per user or recoverable timestamps and recording boundaries | Otherwise no cross-session claim |
| G4 — Baseline reproduction | Official split and author baseline sanity checks | Resolve discrepancies before new claims |
| G5 — Leakage-resistant evaluation | No session/window overlap across partitions; preprocessing fit on train only | Required |
| G6 — Policy comparison | Same split/attacker/utility task across fixed, current-only, history-aware and DP baselines | Required |
| G7 — Statistical support | Grouped confidence intervals, multiple seeds and calibration | Required |
| G8 — Manuscript readiness | Verified references, exact result provenance, null results and limitations | Only then claim empirical contributions |

The correct next milestone is dataset qualification, not writing a results section with synthetic or borrowed benchmark numbers.


## 9. Controller implementation status

A first policy primitive is now implemented in `src/history_controller.py`. It accepts candidate ALLOW/SANITIZE assessments containing:
- calibrated adversarial success risk for the **complete candidate release prefix**;
- estimated legitimate-task utility; and
- estimated latency.

It rejects candidates that violate configured risk, utility or latency constraints, then selects the feasible candidate with the lowest weighted objective. It tracks the last accepted prefix risk and penalizes positive risk growth. It does **not** sum AUC values or per-release risk scores.

This is a policy selector only. It does not train or calibrate the attacker, generate candidate sanitizer assessments, establish DP, or prove a privacy bound. Those estimates must be generated from a validation-only pipeline and then evaluated on held-out data. The controller has unit tests; CI must be checked on the latest commit before the code is described as validated.
